question: A trim tab, deflected opposite to the main control surface's desired holding position, works by:

options.text: Directly moving the main control surface itself via a mechanical link the pilot cannot override
Using its own small aerodynamic force to hold the main control surface at a deflection that balances the aircraft, without the pilot needing to hold continuous control force
Only working when the aircraft is on the ground
Increasing the control surface's mass balance

explanation: A trim tab is deflected against the airflow so that its own small aerodynamic force holds the much larger main control surface at whatever position balances the aircraft, relieving the pilot of the need to hold a continuous control force to maintain that trimmed condition.

question: A "servo tab", as opposed to a simple trim tab, is:

options.text: Moved directly by the pilot, and its own aerodynamic force then moves the otherwise unconnected main control surface — used to reduce pilot effort on large control surfaces
Only used for trimming, never for primary control input
Fixed and never adjustable
Found only on the rudder

explanation: With a servo tab, the pilot's control input moves only the small tab directly; the tab's aerodynamic force then does the work of moving the main control surface, which may otherwise have little or no direct mechanical link to the cockpit controls. This is a way of controlling a large surface without excessive pilot effort.

question: A "spring tab" assists a pilot's control input mainly at:

options.text: Low airspeed, where control forces are lightest
High airspeed, where aerodynamic control forces are greatest — a spring linkage lets the tab deflect more, assisting more, as airload increases
All airspeeds equally, by a fixed, constant amount
Only when the autopilot is engaged

explanation: A spring tab's linkage lets the tab deflect further, providing more assistance, exactly when aerodynamic hinge moments (and therefore control forces) are highest — at high airspeed — while contributing little at low speed, where the unassisted forces are already light.

question: An "anti-balance tab", linked to move in the same direction as the main control surface, is used to:

options.text: Reduce control forces that would otherwise be too light, restoring adequate 'feel' to the controls
Reduce control forces that are too heavy
Prevent flutter
Trim the aircraft automatically

explanation: Deflecting in the same sense as the main surface, an anti-balance tab increases the hinge moment (and therefore the control force) the pilot feels, rather than reducing it — used where a control would otherwise feel unnaturally light, which can itself be a hazard if it lets a pilot inadvertently over-control the aircraft.

question: Deployed symmetrically on both wings, spoiler panels are also used as speed brakes/lift dumpers to:

options.text: Increase lift for takeoff
Increase drag and reduce lift, for a steeper descent or to shorten the landing roll by transferring the aircraft's weight onto the wheels
Increase the critical Mach number
Trim the aircraft in pitch

explanation: Deployed together on both wings (rather than differentially, as for roll control), the same spoiler panels destroy lift and add drag symmetrically — useful for a steeper descent without gaining speed, or after touchdown to 'dump' lift onto the wheels so the brakes and reversers can work effectively.

question: A "flaperon" is a control surface that combines the functions of:

options.text: A flap and an aileron, deflecting together as a flap and differentially as ailerons at the same time
A rudder and an elevator
A slat and a slot
A spoiler and a speed brake, only

explanation: A flaperon serves as both a flap and an aileron: it can droop symmetrically on both wings to act as a flap, while still being deflected differentially, on top of that drooped position, to provide roll control.

question: On a V-tail aircraft, the two tail surfaces — each combining the role of a horizontal and vertical stabilizer — are called "ruddervators" because control inputs are mixed so that:

options.text: Moving them together produces pitch, and moving them differentially produces yaw
Moving them together produces roll only
They only ever move together, never differentially
They have no connection to the rudder pedals or control column at all

explanation: A mixing mechanism converts elevator (pitch) and rudder (yaw) inputs into combined movement of the two V-tail surfaces: moving both surfaces together, in the same sense, produces a pitching moment, while moving them differentially, opposite to each other, produces a yawing moment.

question: An electric trim system that continues running without a pilot command, known as a "trim runaway", is dangerous mainly because:

options.text: It has no effect on control forces
It can move the trim surface to an extreme position, building up a large out-of-trim control force that the pilot must then hold against continuously
It automatically shuts down the engines
It only affects the ailerons

explanation: Because a trim surface is designed to hold a control surface deflected with little or no pilot effort, an uncommanded trim runaway can drive it to a large, uncorrected deflection. The resulting out-of-trim force can become severe enough to demand significant, sustained pilot strength to counter — which is why trim runaway procedures emphasise disconnecting electric trim power promptly.

question: Compared with a manual trim wheel connected by cables directly to the trim tab, an electric trim system:

options.text: Uses a small motor, commanded by a cockpit switch, to drive the same trim mechanism instead of a hand-turned wheel
Has no mechanical connection to any trim surface at all
Can only be used while the autopilot is engaged
Eliminates the need for a trim tab entirely

explanation: Electric trim simply substitutes a small, switch-commanded motor for the pilot's hand on a mechanical trim wheel, driving the same underlying trim tab or stabilizer mechanism — most aircraft with electric trim retain a manual wheel as a backup, since the mechanism being driven is fundamentally the same either way.

question: A simple "mistrim" (trim set incorrectly for the current flight condition) differs from a "trim runaway" in that:

options.text: A mistrim is a static, one-time incorrect setting, while a runaway is trim continuing to move on its own without a pilot command
The two terms describe exactly the same condition
A mistrim always involves the trim motor running continuously
A runaway can only happen with manual trim, never electric trim

explanation: A mistrim is simply trim left at the wrong position for the current speed and configuration — correctable with a normal trim input — while a runaway is a fault condition in which the trim mechanism keeps moving on its own, uncommanded, and calls for isolating trim power rather than just retrimming.

question: A noticeable trim change is generally needed after changing flap setting, extending or retracting the landing gear, or making a significant power change mainly because:

options.text: Each of these changes the balance of pitching moments acting on the aircraft, requiring a different elevator deflection — and therefore a different trim setting — to hold the desired attitude hands-off
None of these actually requires any trim change in practice
Only flap changes ever require a trim change
Trim only needs adjusting once per flight, regardless of configuration changes

explanation: Flaps, gear and power all change the pitching moments acting on the aircraft — flaps and gear aerodynamically, power partly through thrust line effects and slipstream — so each shift in configuration generally calls for a corresponding trim change to keep the aircraft balanced hands-off at the new condition.

question: Rudder trim is particularly useful on a single-engine propeller aircraft at cruise power, and essential on a multi-engine aircraft after an engine failure, mainly because it:

options.text: Relieves the continuous rudder pressure otherwise needed to counteract a steady yawing tendency from propeller/slipstream effects or asymmetric thrust
Has no relationship to yaw or asymmetric thrust at all
Only functions when both engines are producing equal thrust
Replaces the need for rudder pedals entirely

explanation: A steady yawing tendency — whether from propeller effects at cruise power on a single, or from asymmetric thrust after an engine failure on a twin — otherwise requires continuous rudder pressure to counteract. Rudder trim lets that steady correction be held by the trim tab instead, relieving the pilot of a sustained leg force.

question: The technique of "trimming for a speed" relies on the fact that:

options.text: An aircraft trimmed hands-off at a given speed tends to return to that same speed if briefly disturbed, due to its own longitudinal stability
Trim has no relationship to airspeed at all, only to attitude
Trim setting determines engine power directly
An aircraft trimmed at one speed will drift to a random, unrelated speed if disturbed

explanation: Because a statically stable aircraft naturally returns toward its trimmed angle of attack — and therefore its trimmed airspeed — after a disturbance, trimming for a target speed is a genuine, reliable technique: release the controls at the desired speed, and the aircraft's own stability tends to hold, or return to, that speed on its own.

question: While an autopilot is engaged and holding pitch through its own elevator servo, many systems also drive the electric trim automatically, mainly so that:

options.text: The elevator servo is relieved of a sustained load, and the aircraft is left correctly trimmed if the autopilot disconnects
The trim wheel is disabled entirely while the autopilot is engaged
Trim following has no purpose and is purely cosmetic
It prevents the pilot from ever retrimming manually

explanation: If the autopilot's elevator servo alone held a sustained out-of-trim force, disconnecting the autopilot would hand the pilot a large, unexpected control force at that moment. By driving the trim to follow the servo's own effort, the aircraft stays correctly trimmed throughout, so a disconnect is not compounded by a sudden trim surprise.

question: A "speed trim system", found on some swept-wing jet transports, automatically adjusts pitch trim in certain conditions mainly to:

options.text: Compensate for reduced natural speed stability that a swept wing and aft-mounted engines can exhibit at low speed, particularly after takeoff or with an engine inoperative
Replace the need for manual trim entirely in every phase of flight
Only operate at cruise Mach number, never at low speed
Control roll rather than pitch

explanation: Certain swept-wing, aft-engined jet designs can show weaker natural speed stability at low speed than a pilot would otherwise expect, especially with an asymmetric thrust condition. A speed trim system automatically adjusts pitch trim in exactly those conditions to restore more conventional speed-stable handling, without needing constant manual pilot correction.

question: An aileron trim mechanism, found on many aircraft, is used mainly to:

options.text: Relieve a sustained control-wheel force otherwise needed to hold the wings level, due to causes such as a fuel imbalance or minor rigging asymmetry
Provide the aircraft's only means of roll control
Replace the need for a rudder entirely
Only function while the landing gear is extended

explanation: A small, steady difference between the two wings — commonly an uneven fuel load, but also possible rigging tolerances — can require a constant small aileron input to keep the wings level. An aileron trim tab or spring-bias mechanism lets that steady correction be held without continuous pilot effort on the control wheel.

question: Initiating a go-around from an aircraft trimmed nose-up for a slow, flaps-extended approach typically produces:

options.text: A significant nose-up pitching tendency requiring active forward control pressure as power is increased, until the aircraft can be retrimmed for the new, faster, climbing condition
No change in the control force needed at all
A nose-down pitching tendency requiring aft control pressure
An automatic retrim with no pilot action required

explanation: The approach trim setting was chosen for a slow, low-power, nose-up condition. Applying go-around power adds a further nose-up pitching tendency (from thrust line and slipstream effects) on top of that existing trim setting, producing a strong nose-up tendency the pilot must actively counter with forward pressure until the aircraft is retrimmed for the climb.

question: Flying with the rudder trim slightly out of its correct setting for the current condition, even by a small amount, generally:

options.text: Introduces a small, continuous sideslip or rudder deflection that adds unnecessary parasite drag over the course of a flight
Has absolutely no effect on drag or performance
Always improves fuel efficiency
Only matters during takeoff and landing, never in cruise

explanation: An incorrectly set rudder trim holds either a small sideslip angle or an unneeded rudder deflection throughout the flight, both of which add a small but real parasite drag penalty — a minor effect on any single flight, but one airlines take seriously enough to monitor across a fleet for its cumulative fuel cost.

question: On many larger transport aircraft, pitch trim is provided not by a small tab on the elevator but by:

options.text: Adjusting the angle of incidence of the entire horizontal stabilizer itself
A tab mounted on the rudder instead of the elevator
Changing the wing's flap setting
Adjusting engine thrust alone, with no aerodynamic surface involved

explanation: Rather than a small trim tab on the elevator, many larger aircraft trim in pitch by moving the whole horizontal stabilizer to a different angle of incidence — a "trimmable horizontal stabilizer" — which can generate a much larger range of trimming moment than a tab alone, appropriate to a much larger and heavier aircraft.

question: An uncommanded runaway of a trimmable horizontal stabilizer is generally considered more severe than a runaway of a simple elevator trim tab because:

options.text: Moving the whole stabilizer surface produces a much larger pitching moment than a small tab could, building an out-of-trim force more quickly and to a greater magnitude
A stabilizer can never actually run away, unlike a tab
The two produce exactly the same magnitude of pitching moment
A stabilizer runaway has no effect on pitch at all

explanation: Because the whole horizontal stabilizer is a much larger aerodynamic surface than a small elevator trim tab, an uncommanded runaway of the stabilizer builds a pitching moment — and an out-of-trim control force — far more quickly and to a far greater magnitude, which is why stabilizer trim runaway procedures place such emphasis on rapid recognition and immediate trim power isolation.

question: Dedicated electric trim cutout switches are provided in the cockpit mainly so that, in the event of a trim runaway, the pilot can:

options.text: Isolate electrical power to the trim motor directly, stopping the runaway without needing to diagnose the exact cause
Increase the speed of the trim motor
Only be used to test the trim system on the ground
Reverse the direction of the autopilot

explanation: Rather than requiring the crew to work out exactly why trim is running away, dedicated cutout switches let them immediately remove electrical power from the trim motor, stopping the uncommanded movement — a simple, fast, and deliberately robust response to a fault whose exact cause may not be known in the moment.

question: A cockpit trim position indicator is checked before takeoff mainly to:

options.text: Confirm the trim is set within the normal takeoff range, since a grossly mis-set trim can cause serious pitch control difficulty during rotation and initial climb
Show the current outside air temperature
Indicate engine oil pressure
Confirm the landing gear is retracted

explanation: Because trim position directly affects the elevator (or stabilizer) force needed to rotate and control pitch during takeoff, checking that the trim indicator reads within the normal takeoff range beforehand is a deliberate safeguard against a mis-set trim causing a serious pitch upset right at the most speed- and altitude-limited part of the flight.

question: Taking off with trim set to an extreme nose-up position, well outside the normal range, risks:

options.text: An excessively early or abrupt pitch-up at rotation, potentially exceeding the pilot's ability to control the resulting attitude
Making rotation completely impossible
No effect whatsoever on the takeoff
Only affecting the aircraft after landing

explanation: An extreme nose-up trim setting adds its own strong pitching moment on top of whatever elevator input the pilot applies at rotation, which can produce an unexpectedly early, rapid, or excessive pitch-up — a documented cause of serious takeoff accidents, and exactly why trim setting is verified before every takeoff.

question: An unequal fuel quantity between the left and right wing tanks typically requires:

options.text: A small, steady aileron trim input to counter the resulting rolling tendency toward the heavier wing
No control input of any kind, since fuel imbalance has no aerodynamic effect
A rudder trim change only, never an aileron trim change
Immediately shutting down an engine

explanation: A heavier wing (from more fuel remaining in that tank) tends to roll the aircraft toward that side under gravity, requiring a small, steady opposite aileron input to hold the wings level — exactly the sustained, low-level correction that an aileron trim mechanism is meant to relieve the pilot from holding by hand.
